title: XP Are there any resources available on running Windows 2003, XP , and/or VXAce on Linux?

posts.author: 0gits
posts.body: To clarify, I'm not referring to running games made in these engines. I looked online but couldn't find much. That's why I'm asking here. Are there any launch commands (brought them on Steam), external tools, or patches that would help the process of making games in them? I don't want to necessarily rely on anything that would break compatibility when running the exported project natively on Windows. Any suggestions, answers, or links to forum posts related to this would be appreciated.

posts.author: kyonides
posts.body: You'd need either a Ruby script to implement Win32api on Linux that should be ignored if running natively on Windows OR use a custom engine like mkxp, mkxp-z or hiddenchest, and others.

0gits said:

Click to expand...
Cool. So here are the steps you need to go through. As I understand it, you bought RPG Maker through Steam, correct? If so, then you can just use Proton, which is Wine on steroids and customized for gaming. I assume you know the basics of usage regarding Wine/Proton. If not, please say so.
Set the current Proton version for RPG Maker in the compatibility settings. It's 9.0.4 at the moment.
Install RPG Maker
That's it, to be honest. Now... the actual difficulty people have is playing midi files. There are two options for you. You can convert all RTP midi files into ogg or mp3 and not use any midi files in your project and be done with it. Alternatively, if you want to use midi files, follow the next steps.
For simplicity, install Protontricks and open your terminal.
Type
Code:
protontricks -l
This will give you a list of all installed Steam games with their specific APPID. Make a note of the APPID from your installed RPG Maker.
Type
Bash:
protontricks your-rpgmaker-appid -q directmusic dsdmo
This will download and install needed components to get audio with midi working correctly.
Download this old DirectX redistributable package from Microsoft.
https://web.archive.org/web/20060509081637/http://download.microsoft.com/download/4/7/5/475cc4c2-09bb-4d7f-b7c9-b11750b45604/directx_9c_Aug05sdk_redist.exe
Extract the redistributable package with e.g. 7z. You can do this in the terminal like so:
Bash:
7z e your-redistributable-package o./extracted-package
This will extract it into the newly created directory "extracted-package" in the same working directory.
Go into the extracted package. There you will se a bunch of files. We need the "DirectX.cab" one. Open it with the archive app of your choice and extract the "gm16.dls" file. Alternatively, you can also do this with e.g. 7z in the terminal. Like so:
Bash:
7z e DirectX.cab gm16.dls
Rename the extracted "gm16.dls" file into "gm.dls".
Copy the "gm.dls" file into
For 32 bit - > drive_c/Windows/system32/drivers/
For 64 bit - > drive_c/Windows/syswow64/drivers/
in your specific prefix. Create the "drivers" directory if necessary.
You are good to go.

If you're working on a PC, the RTP will be installed automatically as intended. On laptops the story might be a bit different. Especially on (very) old laptops or ones with low free RAM. There it might install, yet, Steam might not recognize it immediately, even after reinstall. There you'd have to rely on some manual tricks, not proton related AFAIK, to let it find the RTP directory path it picked during install.
Possible compatibility issues if using community-made replacements
case
statement syntax might fail because they include stuff like
when 1 : call_method
In that case you'd need to replace : with keyword then or keep
when 1
and
call_method / an algorithm
on separate lines.
method_name[white space][parenthesis]argument[parenthesis] like hi! (set_name)
You'd have to remove the white space ASAP.
Issues with Win32API calls that are Windows-exclusive, they just don't exist on Linux.

posts.author: schM0ggi
posts.body:
0gits said:
I see. Thank you. Would you recommend the community replacements?
Click to expand...
Depends on the use case. For you as a developer, I'd recommend it if you are not scared of digging a bit into documentation to fully understand how to use all the new stuff it offers. Of course, you can always just use it for the updated backend and its performance boost, but even for only that it doesn't hurt to read some of the documentation. The wiki on the github repo is very informative and a good place to start. Their Discord is also a nice place to get some support and ask questions if needed.
In the end, it all comes down to your planned scale. The underlying hood of the older RPG Maker products is old... very old. While it's fine to do games with it, you can run fast into performance problems and/or limits when trying to get "ambiguous" due to old ruby version and some bad coded standard scripts (like collision checking). Using community replacements like mkxp-z gives you a lot more performance, hardware acceleration, modern resolutions and features from newer Makers (like blur background etc.). Though, the bad coded standard scripts remain, the performance hit is not noticeable in general because of the great performance gain you get. But I still suggest, if one is skilled enough in coding, to invest time improving some of the standard code or use ready to use scripts from the community to tackle this problems. But I digress, I guess.
Is a community replacement recommended for someone just wanting to play games, especially on other systems than Windows? Depends if the game is leaning on some Win32 API calls or not. If yes, go for Wine/Proton to be on the safe side, otherwise just through in mkxp(-z) and be done with it.

I see, strange. Never encountered such installation problems with the RTP. And I'm using RPG Maker for around 25 years now. I guess something like that can be easily tackled with checking the registry as, if I remember correctly, the path is stored there.
And great hints for possible, even if rare, compatibilty issues that can happen when using stuff like mkxp(-z).
